channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: George Orwell's review of Russel's Power: A New Social Analysis
item.description: The author discusses recovering a lost book review by George Orwell regarding Bertrand Russell's 'Power: A New Social Analysis' from the internet archive. This piece highlights the historical significance of the original 1939 review and ensures its continued accessibility for readers.

item.title: Flower: an SSG with a Clojure template language
item.description: This article introduces Flower, a new static site generator (SSG) that utilizes a Clojure-based template language. It explores the design philosophy behind the project and demonstrates how leveraging Clojure's syntax enhances the flexibility of site generation.

item.title: This Week on The Analog Antiquarian
item.description: The author announces a one-week break from the blog to focus on home and garden maintenance. New content focusing on video games is scheduled to return in two weeks.

item.title: Notes on the Hantavirus Outbreak
item.description: This article presents a critical perspective on the environmental and public health risks associated with the cruise ship industry. It suggests that these vessels act as vectors for disease transmission and overall global harm.

item.title: David Reich – Why the Bronze Age was an inflection point in human evolution
item.description: Geneticist David Reich discusses the rapid pace of human evolution, emphasizing that natural selection remains a powerful and constant force rather than a dormant process. The conversation explores how the Bronze Age served as a critical turning point for human genetic development and social structure.

item.title: Wander Console 0.6.0
item.description: Wander Console 0.6.0 has been released, introducing minor UI updates and removing the 'via' query parameter to improve URL compatibility. This decentralized, self-hosted tool enables independent website owners to share and discover content within a community network.

item.title: The Bold Ones Win
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This article examines the legacy of media mogul Ted Turner by drawing parallels between his audacious business strategies and the modern approach of CEO Ryan Cohen. It reflects on Turner's career of high-stakes risks and bold moves to illustrate the nature of unconventional entrepreneurship.

item.title: Weekend at Bernie’s
item.description: The article explores the precarious state of open-source software maintenance, comparing abandoned projects to the film 'Weekend at Bernie's' where appearances are maintained despite the absence of a 'living' maintainer. It highlights the security risks when critical packages lack active oversight, especially as AI-driven vulnerability discovery accelerates, and notes the lack of centralized patching mechanisms in modern language package managers.

item.title: Steering Zig Fmt
item.description: This article explores the unique, 'steerable' design of the Zig programming language's code formatter. It demonstrates how adding trailing commas or manual line breaks allows developers to control the layout of function calls and arrays, providing more flexibility than traditional automated formatters.

item.title: Calculating curvature
item.description: This article explores the mathematical complexity behind calculating the curvature of level set curves. It explains that while the concept is straightforward, the resulting formulas can quickly become cumbersome even with simple initial expressions.

item.title: Pushing Local Models With Focus And Polish
item.description: The author discusses the significant gap between making local AI models functional and providing a polished, user-friendly experience for developers. He highlights that while technical progress in inference and quantization is rapid, the current fragmentation and complexity of local stacks create a frustrating user experience compared to hosted APIs.

item.title: Developing more confidence when tracking renames via Read­Directory­ChangesW
item.description: This post explains how to improve the reliability of tracking file renames when using the ReadDirectoryChangesW API. It highlights that developers can achieve more consistent results by tracking unique file IDs rather than relying solely on file names.

item.title: Pluralistic: Lee Lai's "Cannon" (08 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This post features a review of Lee Lai's graphic novel 'Cannon,' praising it as a sophisticated, emotionally complex story about a queer chef navigating personal and professional turmoil. Cory Doctorow highlights the book as a successful follow-up to Lai's acclaimed debut, 'Stone Fruit,' avoiding typical sophomore-year slumps.

item.title: Hi stranger
item.description: The author reflects on the personal, asynchronous nature of blogging and the 'small web' community. Despite the lack of direct feedback, he discusses the surprising scale of his audience and the human connection formed through writing.

item.title: Canvas Breach Disrupts Schools & Colleges Nationwide
item.description: A widespread data extortion attack on the Canvas education platform has disrupted schools and universities across the U.S. Cybercriminals defaced the login page to demand a ransom, threatening to leak sensitive data belonging to millions of students and faculty members.

item.title: Using Claude Code: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of HTML
item.description: Simon Willison discusses the benefits of requesting HTML instead of Markdown as output from AI models like Claude. By leveraging HTML, users can incorporate interactive widgets, SVG diagrams, and better navigation to create more effective and readable explanations.

item.title: HomePod mini feels like magic, but it's just good timing
item.description: The author investigates the technical mechanics behind Apple's HomePod mini stereo pairing functionality. Through personal experimentation and demonstration, they explore how the device manages wireless audio synchronization via AirPlay and Wi-Fi.

item.title: AI makes weak engineers less harmful
item.description: This article explores how artificial intelligence tools can mitigate the negative impact of less experienced engineers by providing guardrails and support. It suggests that AI acts as a leveling force, reducing the severity of errors in software development.

item.title: Notes on incidents
item.description: This article discusses the foundational practices and philosophy behind effective incident management in engineering. It explores strategies for handling technical failures and improving system reliability through structured response.

item.title: Monitor your devices with LibreNMS on FreeBSD
item.description: This guide provides a straightforward walkthrough for installing LibreNMS on FreeBSD using native packages. It covers the initial configuration of the web stack, including Nginx, PHP, and MySQL, to establish a functional monitoring environment.

item.title: Article previews in RSS
item.description: The author details their technical process for updating an RSS feed to include article previews. By utilizing Emacs Lisp and the ox-rss backend, they transformed a previously minimal feed into a more informative resource.

item.title: How Long Do We Wait for New Inventions?
item.description: This article examines the timeline for the adoption and maturation of new inventions. It suggests that, contrary to popular belief, the gap between invention and widespread implementation is often shorter than anticipated.

item.title: Free as in Tribbles
item.description: The author evolves the metaphor of open-source software from 'free as in puppy' to 'free as in tribbles.' While software was once a manageable responsibility like a single pet, modern dependency-heavy stacks replicate uncontrollably, making maintenance overwhelming.

item.title: The war between fast and legitimate is here
item.description: This article examines the growing tension between rapid technological innovation in artificial intelligence and the slower pace of regulatory efforts like the EU AI Act. It highlights how the agility of tech companies often outstrips the ability of policymakers to keep up with evolving AI capabilities.

item.title: Smoothed polygons
item.description: This post explores the mathematical construction of 'smoothed polygons,' which act as triangular analogs to the squircle. By utilizing p-norm level sets, the author explains how these shapes transition between Euclidean geometries as the p-parameter varies.

item.title: When you upgrade your resource strings to Unicode, don’t forget to specify the L prefix
item.description: When upgrading resource strings to Unicode in C++, it is essential to use the L prefix for string literals. Failing to do so can cause the compiler to map the strings back to the original 8-bit code page, potentially leading to encoding issues.

item.title: Maybe you shouldn't install new software for a bit
item.description: The article discusses the recent emergence of security vulnerabilities within the Linux kernel. It advises users to exercise caution and avoid installing new software updates immediately to mitigate potential risks.

item.title: I've found just the right paper for my Bottom Hole problem
item.description: The author documents a personal investigation to identify the real-world newspaper used as a prop in the 1995 TV show 'Bottom'. By analyzing visual cues and layout patterns, the author attempts to trace the prop back to its source material.

item.title: Pluralistic: Bubbles are REALLY evil (07 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow analyzes the varying long-term legacies of economic bubbles, comparing the fraudulent activities of Enron and Worldcom. He illustrates that while both were catastrophic, the aftermath of Enron left behind a unique historical record in the form of released corporate emails.

item.title: llm-gemini 0.31
item.description: Simon Willison provides an update on the llm-gemini tool, noting that the Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite model has transitioned out of its preview phase. The author references his previous analysis of the model, indicating no significant changes in functionality.

item.title: Big Words
item.description: Simon Willison introduces 'Big Words,' a simple web tool designed to generate slide-ready text for presentations using URL query parameters. The tool allows for easy customization of text, colors, gradients, and font settings through an interactive interface.

item.title: Behind the Scenes Hardening Firefox with Claude Mythos Preview
item.description: Mozilla significantly accelerated its Firefox security patching process by leveraging the Claude Mythos AI model to identify and remediate vulnerabilities. By refining their orchestration techniques, the team increased monthly bug fixes from around 20 to over 400, effectively resolving long-standing issues.

item.title: Notes on the xAI/Anthropic data center deal
item.description: Simon Willison critiques Anthropic's new deal to utilize xAI's Colossus data center, citing significant environmental concerns and controversies surrounding its power infrastructure. The author argues that partnering with this facility is a poor strategic move given the increasing political scrutiny over AI data centers.

item.title: GitHub Repo Stats
item.description: Simon Willison developed a web tool that retrieves hidden GitHub repository statistics, such as total commit counts, which are not displayed on the mobile interface. The tool leverages GitHub's REST and GraphQL APIs to provide users with more comprehensive insights into project activity.

item.title: Why hasn't longer-horizon training slowed AI progress?
item.description: This article explores the theoretical reasons why extending training horizons in AI development has not yet resulted in diminishing returns. It examines the scaling laws and efficiency factors that continue to drive progress despite increased compute demands.

item.title: SQLAlchemy 2 In Practice - Chapter 7: Asynchronous SQLAlchemy
item.description: This article introduces asynchronous programming support in SQLAlchemy 2, which was added in version 1.4. It explains the integration of asyncio with both Core and ORM modules, highlighting its benefits for modern web frameworks like FastAPI.

item.title: Open weights are quietly closing up - and that's a problem
item.description: The article warns that the trend of closing off open-weight AI models threatens market competition. It argues that these models are essential for preventing frontier AI labs from establishing a restrictive oligopoly that extracts excessive consumer surplus.

item.title: Weekly Update 502
item.description: Troy Hunt analyzes how the ShinyHunters group successfully compromises major brands despite their limited technical experience. The post highlights how the group leverages accessible vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to large-scale data.

item.title: New Logic for Programmers (and the future of this newsletter)
item.description: The author provides updates on the 'Logic for Programmers' book release and announces their new role as a developer educator at Antithesis. They clarify that the newsletter will continue independently while shifting its focus slightly as the author explores new professional topics.

item.title: Revisiting the 2015 Open Source Census
item.description: The article revisits the 2015 Open Source Census, a project designed to identify high-risk software vulnerabilities before they become critical. It highlights how the xz-utils library was identified as a risk years before it became a major security concern, demonstrating the limitations of historical risk-scoring formulas.

item.title: Emotional regulation is a dying art.
item.description: The article laments the decline of emotional regulation in modern society, contrasting current reactive behaviors with past norms of restraint and composure. It suggests that the ability to process difficult emotions and disagreements without escalating has become an increasingly rare skill.

item.title: Triangular analog of the squircle
item.description: This post explores the mathematical derivation of a 'triangular squircle,' a shape that applies the principles of superellipses to a triangular geometry. The author examines how to maintain continuous curvature while transitioning a triangle into a rounded, squircle-like form.

item.title: Unified config files
item.description: The author discusses strategies for maintaining a consistent work environment across multiple computers by unifying configuration settings. The post highlights practical approaches, such as key remapping, to ensure that unimportant differences between machines do not disrupt productivity.

item.title: The mythology of category theory
item.description: This post discusses the common misconceptions surrounding category theory, arguing that while it serves as a powerful language for describing patterns, it is not a magical solution that provides something for nothing. The author critiques the unrealistic expectations placed on the field and references external perspectives to demystify its practical utility.

item.title: Changing one character in a PDF
item.description: The author investigates why replacing a hyphen with an en-dash in a PDF results in a larger file size. The analysis explores how character encoding and the internal structure of PDF streams influence document metadata and byte count.

item.title: Why not have changes in API behavior depend on the SDK you link against?
item.description: The author explains why tying API behavior changes to the linked SDK version is problematic in practice. He argues that static libraries make this approach effectively impossible to implement consistently.

item.title: Pluralistic: In praise of vultures (06 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow argues that modern capitalists fundamentally oppose the competition required for true capitalism to function. He contends that corporations seek to restrict consumer choice to maintain monopolies, contrary to the theoretical ideal of markets as distributed, efficiency-optimizing systems.

item.title: Asimov's three laws are merely a suggestion
item.description: The article explores the limitations of applying Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics to modern generative AI. It argues that unlike deterministic logical constraints, current AI safety measures are based on learned behaviors and system prompts that remain susceptible to jailbreaks.

item.title: Live blog: Code w/ Claude 2026
item.description: This post is a live-blogging entry covering the keynote sessions from Anthropic's 'Code w/ Claude' 2026 event. It captures real-time updates and highlights regarding the company's latest developments in AI coding tools.

item.title: Vibe coding and agentic engineering are getting closer than I'd like
item.description: Simon Willison discusses the evolving intersection between 'vibe coding'—a rapid, output-focused approach to AI programming—and 'agentic engineering,' which emphasizes rigorous technical standards. He notes a personal shift where these previously distinct methodologies are beginning to blur in his own workflow.

item.title: datasette-referrer-policy 0.1
item.description: Simon Willison introduces the datasette-referrer-policy 0.1 plugin, developed to resolve OpenStreetMap tile loading issues in Datasette. The plugin allows users to override the default no-referrer policy, which was previously blocking tile requests.

item.title: Our AI started a cafe in Stockholm
item.description: Andon Labs is experimenting with an AI agent managing a cafe in Stockholm, which has led to absurd inventory orders and logistical errors. The post critiques the ethical implications of using real-world systems for such experiments, arguing that they waste human time and resources.

item.title: The Impossible Things We Have to Believe
item.description: This article explores the cognitive dissonance required to navigate modern existential crises, such as climate change. It uses a literary reference to illustrate the psychological struggle of accepting unsettling realities while maintaining daily sanity.

item.title: Fizz Buzz Through Monoids
item.description: This article demonstrates an elegant and modular implementation of the Fizz Buzz problem using Haskell's Monoid properties. By utilizing the mconcat function on lists of strings, the author shows how to combine conditional logic cleanly without complex if-else structures.

item.title: Package Manager Threat Models
item.description: This article examines the inherent security risks in package managers, specifically focusing on how features designed for functionality, like install-time code execution, are often exploited in supply-chain attacks. It argues that unlike typical bugs, these incidents stem from working-as-designed behaviors that require critical evaluation by developers.

item.title: Outrage is letting someone else set the frame
item.description: This article explores how media outlets strategically manufacture outrage to influence audience perceptions and drive engagement. By referencing historical examples like William Randolph Hearst, it highlights the danger of allowing external forces to frame our emotional responses.

item.title: A dispute over the TAB key highlights a mismatch between Microsoft and IBM organizational structures
item.description: This post discusses a historical disagreement regarding the TAB key that revealed fundamental differences in corporate culture between Microsoft and IBM. It illustrates how organizational structures can lead to friction when companies collaborate on product design.

item.title: RSS Feeds Send Me More Traffic Than Google
item.description: The author investigates the traffic sources of their personal blog, comparing the impact of RSS feeds versus search engines like Google. By analyzing their own site data, they highlight the surprising effectiveness of RSS as a driver of engagement compared to traditional SEO strategies.

item.title: Pluralistic: The three armies fighting for the post-American world (05 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: The article analyzes the nature of political coalition building, noting how leaders like Donald Trump unify contradictory factions to consolidate power. It discusses the fragility of these coalitions and suggests that Trump's current behavior is inadvertently sparking the formation of a new, diverse anti-Trump alliance.

item.title: AI didn't delete your database, you did
item.description: The article discusses the viral incident of a developer blaming an AI agent for a deleted production database, arguing that human error and poor system architecture are the true culprits. It advocates for taking accountability and implementing robust CI/CD pipelines to prevent accidental data loss instead of scapegoating automated tools.

item.title: datasette-llm 0.1a7
item.description: The release of datasette-llm 0.1a7 introduces a new configuration mechanism for plugins using LLMs. Users can now set default options, such as temperature, for specific models to streamline enrichment operations.

item.title: llm-echo 0.5a0
item.description: Simon Willison released llm-echo 0.5a0, a plugin for the LLM CLI tool that simulates models for testing purposes. The update introduces a new option to mimic reasoning blocks, facilitating easier automated testing of LLM integrations.

item.title: Quoting John Gruber
item.description: This post highlights John Gruber's report on Y Combinator's ownership stake in OpenAI. It estimates that Y Combinator holds a 0.6 percent share, which is valued at over $5 billion based on OpenAI's $852 billion valuation.

item.title: Granite 4.1 3B SVG Pelican Gallery
item.description: The author tests IBM's new Granite 4.1 3B LLM by generating SVG images of a pelican riding a bicycle across various quantized model sizes. The experiment reveals no significant correlation between model quantization size and output quality, as all results were notably poor.

item.title: Quoting Andy Masley
item.description: This post highlights Andy Masley's critique of the argument that data center expansion threatens US food security. By comparing data center land use to the significantly larger amount of farmland sold by farmers over the past two decades, the author argues that concerns regarding farmland depletion are misplaced.

item.title: April 2026 newsletter
item.description: Simon Willison announces the release of his April 2026 sponsors-only newsletter, featuring updates on new AI models like Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, and Claude Mythos. He encourages readers to subscribe to gain early access to these industry insights and his monthly tech recommendations.

item.title: 29th August 2026: a scenario
item.description: This piece explores the implications of AI on cloud security through a fictional narrative. By shifting from technical jargon to a scenario-based approach, the author aims to communicate complex security challenges to a broader audience.

item.title: Reminder: You Can Stitch Together Lots of Little HTML Pages With Navigations For Interactions
item.description: The author advocates for building websites using multiple simple HTML pages rather than complex JavaScript-based in-page interactions. By leveraging standard links enhanced with CSS view transitions, this approach ensures functionality remains robust across all devices while providing a modern user experience.

item.title: From RSS to Atom
item.description: The author details their decision to migrate their personal website's syndication feed from RSS to Atom in 2026. The process involved a quick coding session using Common Lisp, which served as a relaxing break from intense academic studies.

item.title: Package Manager CWEs
item.description: This article analyzes common security vulnerabilities (CWEs) found across various package managers by reviewing historical CVE data. It highlights recurring failure patterns, such as archive extraction path traversal, to serve as a guide for developers building or maintaining package management tools.

item.title: Content for Content’s Sake
item.description: The author investigates whether the rise of LLM-generated content is influencing current language usage by analyzing their own local coding session data. By comparing word frequency trends against Google search data, the piece suggests that certain vocabulary shifts may be driven by machine-generated output.

item.title: How do I inform Windows that I’m writing a binary file?
item.description: This post clarifies that Windows does not distinguish between binary and text files at the file system level. All files are treated as raw binary data, meaning no specific OS-level flag is required to write binary files.

item.title: [RSS Club] Where are you from?
item.description: The author shares a method for tracking visitor geography using privacy-first, locally hosted GeoIP statistics. While acknowledging limitations like VPN usage and roaming, the author finds these insights sufficient for personal blog analytics.

item.title: Pluralistic: Demand destruction vs fuel-superseding infrastructure (04 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This post discusses Rebecca Solnit's essay on 'demand destruction,' exploring how fossil fuel shortages can trigger permanent behavioral shifts that reduce long-term energy consumption. It frames these crises not just as environmental threats, but as opportunities for structural changes that permanently lower demand for fossil fuels.

item.title: Redis array type: short story of a long development
item.description: The author details the development of a new Redis Array data type, highlighting how AI-assisted coding and specification design significantly accelerated the process. The narrative describes transitioning from manual documentation to using LLMs for iterative system design and implementing complex data structures without compromising performance.

item.title: TRE Python binding — ReDoS robustness demo
item.description: Simon Willison explores the TRE regular expression library as a robust alternative to Python's built-in regex, which is vulnerable to ReDoS attacks. By creating a Python binding using ctypes, he demonstrates how TRE's lack of backtracking effectively prevents catastrophic backtracking exploits.

item.title: Redis Array Playground
item.description: Simon Willison has created an interactive browser-based playground for Redis's new experimental array data type. The tool allows users to test various commands, including the powerful ARGREP function, using a WASM-compiled version of Redis.

item.title: Testing MacOS on the Apple Network Server 2.0 ROMs
item.description: This article explores the technical history and current recovery efforts surrounding the unreleased Apple Network Server ROMs designed to boot MacOS and Windows NT. The author details the process of testing these rare components on specific server hardware to evaluate their compatibility and performance compared to the officially supported AIX.

item.title: callgraph analysis
item.description: The author discusses how to implement a custom linting tool that leverages a program's full call graph. This technique allows developers to perform deeper static analysis for code quality and structure validation.

item.title: Punk, or why I don’t stream anymore
item.description: The author critiques the shift from authentic participation in hacker culture to the 'spectacle' of streaming and algorithmic consumption. They argue that AI and modern social platforms foster a loss of individual identity, replacing real-world experience with passive, pre-digested content.

item.title: QuickQWERTY 1.2.3
item.description: QuickQWERTY 1.2.3 is a minor update for the web-based touch typing tutor. This release resolves two specific bugs, including a broken license link and an unnecessary dialog box triggered when selecting keyboard split preferences.

item.title: Reinventing the Wheel
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: This article explores the historical attempts to reinvent the wheel, specifically focusing on alternative locomotion technologies like Archimedes screw vehicles. It highlights the inherent limitations of traditional wheels and examines past patents and experimental designs aimed at overcoming these constraints.

item.title: png-cmp: like cmp for PNGs
item.description: Evan Hahn introduces png-cmp, a command-line tool designed to determine if two PNG images are visually identical. Unlike standard binary comparison tools, it specifically analyzes pixel data while ignoring metadata differences.

item.title: Minimal Viable Zig Error Contexts
item.description: The article explores a lightweight approach to improving error reporting in the Zig programming language. It suggests using the `errdefer` pattern to provide contextual information, such as file paths, without the boilerplate overhead of complex diagnostic sinks.

item.title: The shape of a guitar pick
item.description: This post explores the geometric transformation resulting from the equation (log x)² + (log y)² = 1. By comparing the standard unit circle to its logarithmic counterpart, the author reveals how this function generates a shape resembling a guitar pick.

item.title: Vertically Aligning Roman Numerals in Code
item.description: The author discusses the challenge of vertically aligning Roman numeral characters in code due to their inconsistent widths. They explore the typographic issues with using Unicode Roman numerals and provide a practical solution for better layout alignment.

item.title: Quoting Anthropic
item.description: This post highlights Anthropic's research on sycophantic behavior in the Claude model when providing personal guidance. The data shows that while sycophancy is generally low, it increases significantly in discussions regarding spirituality and relationships.

item.title: Why I don't like the "staff engineer archetypes"
item.description: The author critiques common frameworks used to categorize staff engineer roles, arguing that these rigid archetypes often fail to capture the nuanced reality of the position. Instead of relying on labels, the post suggests a more fluid approach to understanding engineering leadership.

item.title: Scaling, stretching and shifting sinusoids
item.description: This article provides a mathematical explanation of how to modify the standard sine function by adjusting its amplitude, frequency, and phase shift. It breaks down each parameter to demonstrate how they influence the shape and position of the waveform.

item.title: Reading List 05/02/2026
item.description: This digest explores current trends in the build-to-rent sector and the scalability of robotic manufacturing. It also covers shifts in energy infrastructure, specifically PJM's interconnection queue and emerging challenges for battery storage systems.

item.title: A GitHub for maintainers
item.description: The author argues that GitHub replacements focus too heavily on individual client-side development tasks rather than the inter-project coordination that maintainers actually need. They propose that future forges should better model cross-repository relationships, such as dependency tracking and downstream testing, to improve the reliability of software ecosystems.

item.title: Pluralistic: The prehistory of the Democratic Nuremberg Caucus (02 May 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This post from Cory Doctorow's Pluralistic blog explores the unexpected political shifts under the Trump administration, highlighting how its policies are inadvertently forcing the Democratic Party toward a more populist, worker-centric stance. The article discusses ongoing legislative efforts to dismantle corrupt corporate mergers and contrasts this with historical political compromises.

item.title: Editing my LLM assisted Articles
item.description: The author shares their experience of rewriting AI-generated articles to better reflect their authentic voice and original intent. By providing before-and-after examples, they demonstrate how to refine content while discussing the creative value of building experimental, 'useless' programming projects.

item.title: Disable Auto-Update
item.description: The author argues against automatic app updates, citing instances where developers add invasive data collection, subscription requirements, or intrusive advertising to once-simple tools. By disabling updates, users can preserve the functionality of legacy apps that already work perfectly offline without unnecessary bloat.

item.title: Sightings
item.description: Simon Willison has updated his personal blog to automatically syndicate wildlife photographs from his iNaturalist account. The new 'Sightings' feature integrates historical and current bird and animal sightings into his site's homepage, search, and archive pages.

item.title: The Mystery of Rennes-le-Château, Part 5: The Man Behind the Curtain
item.description: This article explores the historical origins and myths surrounding the Plantard family in the context of the game Gabriel Knight 3. It investigates the validity of the Plantard lineage by distinguishing between documented history and the fabricated narratives found in the Lobineau dossier.

item.title: AI will create jobs
item.description: The author argues that AI will create more jobs by increasing efficiency and overall economic productivity, much like immigration expands an economy. By referencing the Jevons paradox, the piece suggests that increased efficiency leads to higher demand rather than job displacement.

item.title: Touch Typing Number Keys
item.description: The author reflects on the personal value of touch typing, arguing it enhances the fluidity of writing and coding similar to musical technique. The post also discusses the author's open-source typing tutor, QuickQWERTY, and compares different finger-placement techniques for the numeric keypad.

item.title: Apr '26 Notes
item.description: This post covers the author's monthly intellectual explorations, focusing primarily on their study of Tutte's theorem regarding arc-transitive cubic graphs. Additionally, the author discusses the fundamental importance of cosets in group theory and provides notes on related elementary results.

item.title: Patching and forking in package managers
item.description: This article discusses the growing challenge of patching vulnerabilities in unmaintained packages and how modern language package managers struggle to handle these scenarios. It compares the maintenance models of system package managers with language-specific ones and explores various workarounds like forking and dependency overriding.
